L0@P0: Smooth Riemannian Structures on Dessins
L1@P0: d’Enfants
L2@P0: Jean-Marie Morvan
L3@P0: May 23, 2022
L4@P0: Abstract
L5@P0: We show how to define a canonical Riemannian metric on a ”dessin
L6@P0: d’enfants” drawn on a topological surface. This gives a possible explanation
L7@P0: of a claim of A. Grothendieck [7].
L8@P0: In his famous paper Esquisse d’un programme [7], Alexandre Grothendieck
L9@P0: introduced a new view point in the study of maps on surfaces (that he called
L10@P0: dessins d’enfants). At the end of this text, insisting on the interest to pursue
L11@P0: his ideas, he briefly pointed out a link with Riemannian geometry:
L12@P0: ”Depuis 1977, dans toutes les questions (comme dans ces deux derniers
L13@P0: th`emes que je viens d’´evoquer) o`u interviennent des cartes bidimensionelles,
L14@P0: la possibilit´e de les r´ealiser canoniquement sur une surface conforme, donc
L15@P0: sur une courbe alg´ebrique complexe dans le cas orient´e compact, reste en filigrane constant dans ma r´eflexion. Dans pratiquement tous les cas (en fait,
L16@P0: tous les cas sauf celui de certaines cartes sph´eriques avec ”peu d’automorphismes”) une telle r´ealisation conforme implique en fait une m´etrique riemanienne canonique, ou du moins, canonique `a une constante multiplicative
L17@P0: pr`es.”
L18@P0: [”Since 1977, in all the questions (such as the two last themes evoked above)
L19@P0: where two-dimensional maps occur, the possibility of realising them canonically on a conformal surface, so on a complex algebraic curve in the compact oriented case, remains constantly in filigree throughout my reflection.
L20@P0: In practically every case (in fact, in all cases except that on certain spherical maps with ”few automorphisms”) such a conformal realisation implies
L21@P0: in fact a canonical Riemannian metric, or at least, canonical up to a multiplicative constant.”]
L22@P0: Two statements in these lines could be clarified : First of all, A. Grothendieck
L23@P0: does not specify the regularity of the canonical metric. Moreover, the notion
L24@P0: of ”map with few automorphisms” is not precisely defined.
L25@P0: 1
L26@P0-1: arXiv:1706.09158v2 [math.DG] 22 Sep 2017• A priori, to find a Riemannian metric canonically associated to a dessin
L27@P1: D on a surface X, one could build a triangulation associated to the
L28@P1: dessin, endow this triangulation with a piecewise linear structure, and
L29@P1: then, build the (singular) Euclidean metric defined by affecting the
L30@P1: length 1 to each edge. Such a metric is not smooth in general (only
L31@P1: continuous, since it may have conical singularities at the vertices).
L32@P1: This construction does not need any restriction on the automorphism
L33@P1: group of the dessin.
L34@P1: • These considerations lead to look for a smooth canonical metric associated to the dessin D. The natural way is to build the standard
L35@P1: conformal (that is, complex) structure associated to D, and then to
L36@P1: consider Riemannian metrics invariant by the group Aut(X) of biholomorphisms of X. The Poincare-Klein-Koebe uniformisation theorem
L37@P1: gives a Riemannian metric with constant Gaussian curvature in the
L38@P1: conformal class of Riemannian metrics defined on X. This Riemannian metric is unique if the genus of X is strictly greater than 1, unique
L39@P1: up to a scaling constant if the genus is 1, and invariant by the group
L40@P1: Aut(X) of biholomorphisms of X. However, this construction fails if
L41@P1: the genus of X is 0. In this situation, X is biholomorphic to the Riemann sphere Cˆ, the modular space of X is reduced to a point and a
L42@P1: dessin does not induce any information on the conformal structure of
L43@P1: X. Moreover, the standard metric with constant Gaussian curvature 1
L44@P1: in the Riemann sphere is not invariant by the group Aut(Cˆ) of biholomorphisms of Cˆ. In order to find a canonical metric associated to a
L45@P1: dessin drawn on Cˆ, the idea is to replace the (too large) group Aut(Cˆ)
L46@P1: by the (finite) subgroup of biholomorphisms Aut(Cˆ, D) that preserve
L47@P1: D and to build a Riemannian metric invariant only by Aut(Cˆ, D). We
L48@P1: propose two different constructions.
L49@P1: – The first one is based on the average (over Aut(Cˆ, D)) of the
L50@P1: metrics obtained by pullback of the standard metric of the round
L51@P1: 2-sphere of radius 1. We can build this metric without any restrictions on Aut(Cˆ, D). However, its Gaussian curvature is not
L52@P1: constant in general.
L53@P1: – The second one mimics the hyperbolic situation, but excludes
L54@P1: the case where Aut(Cˆ, D) is cyclic. The metric we get is invariant by Aut(Cˆ, D) and of constant Gaussian curvature 1. The
L55@P1: opinion of the author is that it may be the one considered by A.
L56@P1: Grothendieck, who excluded in his text, ”certain spherical maps
L57@P1: with ”few automorphisms””, although he did not mention that
L58@P1: he looked for a metric with constant Gaussian curvature.
L59@P1: In both case, these metrics coincide with the standard metric of the
L60@P1: round sphere S
L61@P1: 2 of radius 1 when Aut(Cˆ, D) is a subgroup of SO(3).
L62@P1-2: 2Let us now state the theorem corresponding to the second construction
L63@P2: (the (non smooth) continuous situation is mentioned in section 8, and the
L64@P2: result corresponding to the first construction is stated in section 12.2), see
L65@P2: notations and definitions below :
L66@P2: Theorem 1 Let (X, D) be a dessin on a (closed oriented) topological surface.
L67@P2: • If gX > 1, then (X, D) admits a canonical Riemannian metric with
L68@P2: constant Gaussian curvature −1 induced by D, invariant by Aut(X).
L69@P2: • If gX = 1, then (X, D) admits a canonical Riemannian flat metric
L70@P2: induced by D, unique up to a scaling constant, invariant by Aut(X).
L71@P2: • If gX = 0 and Aut(X, D) is not cyclic, then (X, D) admits a canonical Riemannian metric of constant Gaussian curvature 1 invariant by
L72@P2: Aut(X, D). In particular, if Aut(X, D) is a subgroup of SO(3) (canonically embedded in P SL(2, C)), this metric coincides with the standard
L73@P2: metric of the round 2-sphere of radius 1.
L74@P2: This text trying to be as self contained as possible, we present in the following paragraphs some backgrounds on conformal geometry, Riemannian
L75@P2: geometry and the theory of dessins d’enfants. Many results of this paper
L76@P2: are simple reminders (in particular in Riemannian geometry, conformal geometry and complex analysis) fixing the notations and giving the essential

L47: ## Abstract
L48: 
L49: It is known that every finite group can be represented as the full group of automorphisms of a suitable compact dessin d’enfant. In this paper, we give a constructive and easy proof that the same holds for any countable group by considering non-compact dessins. Moreover, we show that any tame action of a countable group is so realisable.

L69: ## 1 Introduction
L70: 
L71: In this paper, all surfaces are assumed to be orientable, connected, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. If X is a surface, then we denote by \(\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) the group of its orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms. A topological action (or just an action) of an abstract group G on a surface X is an injective homomorphism \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) such that \(\theta (G)\) acts tame on X (see Sect. 【26†2】).
L72: Every surface admits a Riemann surface structure and, if S is a Riemann surface different from the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, the punctured plane, a torus, an annulus, the hyperbolic plane or the punctured hyperbolic plane, then its group \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\) of conformal automorphisms is a countable group.
L73: Conversely, in [【27†8】], Greenberg proved that for every countable (finite or infinite) group G there is a Riemann surface S (which can be assumed to be compact if G is finite) and an injective homomorphism \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(S)\). Moreover, \(\theta \) may be assumed to be an isomorphism (by using maximal Fuchsian groups). A short proof of the previous fact has been given by Allcock in [【28†1】] (see also [【29†15】]).
L74: In the case that S is hyperbolic, its universal cover is the hyperbolic plane \({\mathbb {H}}^{2}\). The hyperbolic metric of \({\mathbb {H}}^{2}\) induces a complete Riemannian metric of constant negative curvature on S and it holds that its group \(\mathrm{Isom}^{+}(S)\) of orientation-preserving isometries coincides with \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\).
L75: A dessin d’enfant (or just a dessin) is a pair \({\mathcal D}=(X,{\mathcal G})\), where X is a surface (either compact or not), \({\mathcal G} \subset X\) is a bipartite graph (vertices are either black or white and adjacent ones have different colors) where each vertex has finite degree and each connected component of \(X \smallsetminus {\mathcal G}\), called a face, is homeomorphic to an open disc and bounded by a finite set of edges (an edge might be internal to a face).
L76: Each dessin d’enfant on X induces a unique (up to biholomorphisms) Riemann surface structure on it [【30†5】, 【31†12】]. Dessins, on a compact surface X, were first introduced by Grothendieck in his Esquisse d’un Programme (1984) [【32†9】] (we call these dessins as Grothendieck’s dessins).
L77: In this case, such a Riemann surface structure can be described by an algebraic curve defined over the field of algebraic numbers \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) and Grothendieck’s idea was to use such a combinatorial tool to obtain information on the structure of the absolute Galois group \(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/{\mathbb Q})\). Generalities on Grothendieck’s dessins can be found, for instance, in [【30†5】,【33†6】,【34†7】, 【32†9】, 【31†12】].
L78: The mapping class group associated to X is defined to be \(\mathrm{Map}(X)=\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)/\mathrm{Hom}_{0}(X)\), where \(\mathrm{Hom}_{0}(X)\) is the subgroup of homeomorphisms which are isotopic to the identity. Let \(\theta :\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X) \rightarrow \mathrm{Map}(X)\) denote the quotient group projection.
L79: The automorphisms of the bipartite graph \({\mathcal G}\), denoted by \(\mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\), is the group consisting of automorphisms of the graph that keep invariant black (respectively, white) vertices (called automorphisms of the bipartite graph).
L80: Let \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathcal D})\) be the subgroup of \(\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) consisting of those \(\phi \in \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) keeping invariant \({\mathcal G}\) and inducing an element of \(\mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\). Note that, by performing any isotopy of \(\phi \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathcal D})\) relative the vertices and keeping invariant the edges, we obtain the same automorphism of the bipartite graph; so this group is always uncountable.
